explanations.answer: Sends him a messenger with a threat
explanations.explanation: Right after Ahab tells her everything, Jezebel sends a messenger to Elijah with these words: “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely, if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the lives of those you killed!” (1 Kings 19:1-2). The message is a threat with a deadline. That is a lot of heat for one delivery.

No soldiers show up in this passage. The text says Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah (1 Kings 19:2). Her message is a promise about what she will do by this time tomorrow. A messenger carries words, and the words here are the threat.

explanations.answer: Sends him a gift to make peace
explanations.explanation: Nothing about peace comes in that messenger's hands. Jezebel's message is an oath: “May the gods deal with me, and ever so severely…” (1 Kings 19:2). No card, no bow, no peace offering. Whatever was in that delivery, you would not want to sign for it.

The text says it plainly: “…Elijah was afraid and ran for his life.” (1 Kings 19:3). This is the prophet who stood on Mount Carmel against Baal's prophets (1 Kings 18:20-40). I think fear can hit hard even after a big moment. The Bible doesn't hide it.

The text says the opposite. “…Elijah was afraid and ran for his life.” (1 Kings 19:3). Elijah, the LORD's prophet, had just stood on Mount Carmel against Baal's prophets (1 Kings 18:20-40). So this is a surprise turn, and I'd have asked him to repeat that part too.

explanations.answer: A day's journey into the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Elijah leaves his servant in Beersheba, a town in Judah, “…while he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness.” (1 Kings 19:3-4). Notice he goes out alone. A servant left behind and an empty stretch of wilderness ahead. That is a quiet, lonely picture.

Jezreel never comes up in this passage. The text says Elijah went “…a day’s journey into the wilderness.” (1 Kings 19:4). He leaves his servant in Beersheba first (1 Kings 19:3). So the wilderness is where the text sends him, not back to Jezreel.

Carmel is where Elijah faced Baal's prophets (1 Kings 18:20-40), but he doesn't go back there. After Beersheba, “…he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness.” (1 Kings 19:4). That is the opposite direction from a victory lap.

Elijah “…prayed that he might die.” (1 Kings 19:4). His words were, “I have had enough, LORD… Take my life, for I am no better than my fathers.” This is a heavy moment, and I think it hurts to read. Notice that he says it to the LORD, out loud.
He doesn't ask for that. Elijah prays something much heavier. He prays “…that he might die.” (1 Kings 19:4). I think this one hurts, and the text lets us see it plainly.

explanations.answer: That the rain would keep falling
explanations.explanation: Rain isn't what he prays about here. Under the broom tree, Elijah “…prayed that he might die.” (1 Kings 19:4). He says, “I have had enough, LORD…” It's a heavy prayer, and the text doesn't dress it up.

The text doesn't say that. Elijah left his servant in Beersheba (1 Kings 19:3), and the one who touches Elijah is an angel (1 Kings 19:5). No servant walks up on this scene. So what wakes Elijah is not a person from home.

Right, no servant here. Elijah left him in Beersheba (1 Kings 19:3). It is an angel who touches Elijah and says, “Get up and eat.” (1 Kings 19:5). Elijah is alone out there, and still someone reaches him.
There by his head is “…a cake of bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water.” (1 Kings 19:6). Baked over hot coals, and I respect that. Anything fresh from the heat gets my attention.

Figs are not what the text says. By Elijah's head is “…a cake of bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water.” (1 Kings 19:6). That is bread, fresh from the coals. I will say I like the fig guess, since it sounds like good wilderness food.

Raisins are one of my favorite toppings, but they are not what's by Elijah's head. The text says “…a cake of bread baked over hot coals, and a jar of water.” (1 Kings 19:6). Bread and water are what the text names. I'll keep the raisins for my own cookies.

It happens. “A second time the angel of the LORD returned and touched him…” (1 Kings 19:7). Elijah had already eaten, drunk and lain back down (1 Kings 19:6). So the angel comes back and tells him to get up and eat again. This time the angel adds, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” (1 Kings 19:7).

The text says otherwise. “A second time the angel of the LORD returned and touched him…” (1 Kings 19:7). Elijah had eaten, drunk and lain down again (1 Kings 19:6). Then the angel returns, so there is a second touch.

explanations.answer: The journey will be too much for him
explanations.explanation: The angel says, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” (1 Kings 19:7). That is the reason the angel gives, so we can say it. The food is for the journey. I think the food is meant to carry him.

explanations.answer: Jezebel's messenger is about to find him
explanations.explanation: The angel doesn't mention Jezebel or her messenger. The reason given is, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” (1 Kings 19:7). The angel is talking about the road ahead. That is the whole reason.

explanations.answer: His servant is coming to take him home
explanations.explanation: The text mentions no one coming to take Elijah home. The angel says, “Get up and eat, or the journey will be too much for you.” (1 Kings 19:7). The reason given is the journey. That is what the text gives.

Elijah “…walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.” (1 Kings 19:8). Moses, Israel's leader, met God at a burning bush there (Exodus 3:1-4). That is a long walk, and the food gave him strength for it. Forty days is a lot of road.

Carmel is where Elijah faced Baal's prophets (1 Kings 18:20-40), but it isn't where this walk ends. The text says he walked “…until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.” (1 Kings 19:8). Horeb is where God called to Moses, Israel's leader, from a burning bush (Exodus 3:1-4). So the walk takes him somewhere holy.

Tabor is not named in this passage. Elijah “…walked forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.” (1 Kings 19:8). Moses, Israel's leader, heard God call from a burning bush at that mountain (Exodus 3:1-4). So Horeb is the stop.

explanations.answer: He is the only one left
explanations.explanation: Elijah says, “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.” (1 Kings 19:10). That is how he describes his situation to the LORD. I think he feels very alone. Hold on to that line, because it comes back later.
Elijah says nothing like that. He says, “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.” (1 Kings 19:10). He doesn't mention any friends. I think he feels completely alone.

explanations.answer: He will go back and fight
explanations.explanation: Fighting isn't what he says here. His words are, “I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well.” (1 Kings 19:10). It is the LORD who later tells him to go back (1 Kings 19:15). Elijah is telling the LORD where he stands.

The text says it directly: “…a great and mighty wind tore into the mountains and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind.” (1 Kings 19:11). That is a LOT of wind, and it is still not Him. A wind that shatters rocks, and the LORD still wasn't in it.

The text says the opposite. “…a great and mighty wind tore into the mountains and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind.” (1 Kings 19:11). Big and loud, and yet not where He was. The wind passes before Him, and that's all.

The text says the opposite. “After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire.” (1 Kings 19:12). So the fire does not hold Him. Wind, earthquake and fire all come, and none of them is where He is.

Yes. “After the earthquake there was a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire.” (1 Kings 19:12). The wind and the earthquake came first, and He wasn't in those either. That is the third big thing in a row, and none of them was Him. I've been near plenty of ovens, so I can tell you fire gets all the attention.
“…after the fire came a still, small voice.” (1 Kings 19:12). After all that noise, it is quiet. I love that the text lets the quiet land. Wind, earthquake, fire, and then a whisper of a sound.
No flash of light here. The text says, “…after the fire came a still, small voice.” (1 Kings 19:12). After the loud things, something soft arrives. It's the opposite of a flash.
There is no water in this scene. What comes after the fire is “…a still, small voice.” (1 Kings 19:12). It's quiet, not roaring. After all that roar, the quiet is the surprise.

explanations.answer: Wraps his face in his cloak and steps out
explanations.explanation: “When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave.” (1 Kings 19:13). He doesn't stay hidden. He covers his face, and still goes out to stand there. That says a lot about how he took in that voice.

explanations.answer: Runs deeper into the back of the cave
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other direction. Elijah “…wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave.” (1 Kings 19:13). He comes toward the entrance, not away from it. He covers his face and steps out.

explanations.answer: Falls facedown and stays inside the cave
explanations.explanation: That is not what the text says. Elijah “…wrapped his face in his cloak and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave.” (1 Kings 19:13). He is standing, not on the ground, and he goes out to the mouth of the cave. He covers his face and steps out.

explanations.answer: He says the same thing he said the first time
explanations.explanation: Elijah answers with the same words: “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts… I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well” (1 Kings 19:14). They match what he said in verse 10. The text doesn't say why he repeats it, so I won't guess too hard. I will say the answer comes out word for word.

explanations.answer: He says he is ready to go back to Israel
explanations.explanation: That is not in his answer. He repeats what he said before: “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts… I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well” (1 Kings 19:14). The word about going back comes from the LORD next (1 Kings 19:15).

explanations.answer: He says he is sorry he ran from Jezebel
explanations.explanation: No sorry here. Elijah gives the same answer he gave before: “I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts… I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well” (1 Kings 19:14). He says nothing about running. Same answer, same words.

The LORD says to anoint “…Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to succeed you as prophet.” (1 Kings 19:16). So Elisha, a man from Abel-meholah, is the one set to take over as prophet. The work is meant to go on past Elijah. I like that the LORD has a plan for what comes next.

The text doesn't call Elisha a priest. The LORD says to anoint “…Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel-meholah to succeed you as prophet.” (1 Kings 19:16). He is to follow Elijah, as prophet. That is the job that gets passed on.
Judge is not what the LORD says. Elisha is to be anointed “…to succeed you as prophet.” (1 Kings 19:16). Elijah is the prophet he is stepping in for. That is the role.

The LORD says the opposite. “Nevertheless, I have reserved seven thousand in Israel…” and they are the ones whose knees have not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Elijah had said, “I am the only one left…” (1 Kings 19:14). So the LORD names seven thousand where Elijah said he was the only one.

Right. The LORD says, “…I have reserved seven thousand in Israel…” and those are the ones whose knees have not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:18). Elijah had said, “I am the only one left…” (1 Kings 19:14). Seven thousand is quite a number for one lonely prophet.

“Elijah passed by him and threw his cloak around him.” (1 Kings 19:19). The cloak is the thing the text gives. Elijah passes by, and the cloak goes around Elisha. That is a bold way to make an introduction.
The text doesn't mention a belt. It says Elijah “…threw his cloak around him.” (1 Kings 19:19). The cloak goes around Elisha as Elijah passes by. A belt would have been a very different move.
A rope isn't in the story. Elijah “…passed by him and threw his cloak around him.” (1 Kings 19:19). The cloak is the thing. I'm glad it wasn't a rope, because that would be a different scene.

explanations.answer: To kiss his father and mother goodbye
explanations.explanation: Elisha says, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you.” (1 Kings 19:20). That is his one request. Elijah answers, “Go on back…” and asks, “for what have I done to you?” Elisha asks to say goodbye first, and he says he will follow.

explanations.answer: To finish plowing the whole field first
explanations.explanation: Plowing isn't what he asks for. Elisha says, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you.” (1 Kings 19:20). One request, and it is about his parents. The field can wait.

explanations.answer: To bring his brothers along with him
explanations.explanation: Brothers aren't mentioned in his request. Elisha says, “Please let me kiss my father and mother goodbye, and then I will follow you.” (1 Kings 19:20). The ask is about saying goodbye to his father and mother. That is all he asks.

explanations.answer: Slaughters them and feeds the people
explanations.explanation: Elisha “…took his pair of oxen, and slaughtered them.” and then “…cooked the meat and gave it to the people, and they ate.” (1 Kings 19:21). The oxen were the team he was plowing with (1 Kings 19:19), and he gives the meat to the people. I think that is a big way to head out the door.

explanations.answer: Gives them to his father to keep
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Elisha “…took his pair of oxen, and slaughtered them.” and “…cooked the meat and gave it to the people, and they ate.” (1 Kings 19:21). The meat goes to the people. His father isn't mentioned here.

explanations.answer: Sells them to pay for the journey
explanations.explanation: No selling happens. Elisha “…took his pair of oxen, and slaughtered them.” and “…cooked the meat and gave it to the people, and they ate.” (1 Kings 19:21). He feeds people instead of collecting money. The text doesn't say what he got out of it.

Yes. “Then he set out to follow and serve Elijah.” (1 Kings 19:21). Elisha had cooked the meat and given it to the people, and they ate. After that, Elisha goes after Elijah. Elijah, the man who ran, now has someone who set out to follow and serve him.
The text says otherwise. “Then he set out to follow and serve Elijah.” (1 Kings 19:21). After the people eat, that is the next thing the text says about Elisha. He sets out to follow and serve.
